lead: One cable or fibre carries far more than one signal needs. Multiplexing shares that capacity: a multiplexer (mux) at the sending end puts many signals onto one link, and a demultiplexer (demux) separates them at the receiving end. Split the frequency band and every user sends all the time in its own slice (FDM, and its optical twin WDM). Split time instead and each user gets the whole link for a short turn (TDM). Trunks, cable TV and fibre backbones work this way.
prereq: You need: 2.1 for sampling and bit rates, 2.3 for bandwidth, and 2.6 for carriers and modulation.

blocks.text: Frequency Division Multiplexing (FDM) shares the link by frequency. Each signal is modulated onto its own carrier (see 2.6), and the carriers are placed so their bands sit side by side without overlapping. Every user transmits at once, confined to its own slice; the receiver's tuning dial is the demultiplexer that selects one band and rejects the rest.

A guard band is a small unused strip of spectrum between neighbouring channels. Real filters cannot cut off sharply, so without a gap one channel leaks into the next. Guard bands cost bandwidth and buy isolation.

blocks.where: B<sub>total</sub> is the total bandwidth the link must provide, in Hz; B<sub>i</sub> is the bandwidth of channel i, in Hz; n is the number of channels; B<sub>guard</sub> is the width of one guard band, in Hz. With n equal channels of bandwidth B: B<sub>total</sub> = nB + (n − 1)B<sub>guard</sub>.

blocks.text: FDM runs broadcasting and the old analog telephone network. Each radio station, TV channel and mobile operator holds a licensed band, and all transmit at once. In the analog telephone hierarchy, 12 voice channels are stacked into a 48 kHz group and five groups make a 240 kHz supergroup. The 4 kHz per channel is the channel spacing and already includes the guard band between neighbouring voice channels, so 12 × 4 kHz needs no extra gap.

Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) shares the link by time. The link runs at full speed, but each user gets all of it for a short turn. In synchronous TDM the turns repeat in a fixed pattern called a frame: one complete round of slots, where slot i of every frame belongs to user i.

The frame rate must match the sources. A digitised voice channel delivers one 8-bit sample every 125 µs, that is 8000 samples per second (see 2.1). So the multiplexer builds 8000 frames per second, each 125 µs long.

One framing bit per frame marks where a frame starts. Without it a lost bit would push every channel's data into its neighbour's slot. When inputs run at slightly different clock rates, the mux inserts extra bits into a slow channel's slot and the demux removes them; this is bit stuffing (pulse stuffing).

A T-1 frame carries 24 channels: 24 × 8 + 1 = 193 bits at 8000 frames/s, giving 1.544 Mbit/s. An E-1 frame has 32 slots of 8 bits: 32 × 8 = 256 bits at 8000 frames/s, giving 2.048 Mbit/s, with 30 voice slots and 2 for framing and signalling.

Statistical (asynchronous) TDM gives a slot only to a user who has data. Because slots go on demand, each must carry an address so the demux knows whose bytes these are. It serves more users than it has slots and suits bursty computer traffic.

sections.h3: WDM: FDM on light, and the comparison

blocks.text: Wavelength Division Multiplexing (WDM) is FDM performed on light. A fibre carries several beams of different wavelength (colour) at once. A prism or grating at the mux bends each beam into the same fibre, and a matching prism at the demux bends them apart. Because f = c/λ, splitting by wavelength is splitting by frequency: c is the speed of light in the fibre in m/s, λ the wavelength in m, f the frequency in Hz.

Dense WDM (DWDM) packs wavelengths closely, for example 100 GHz apart on the grid near 1550 nm, where fibre loss is lowest. Each wavelength carries its own high-speed channel, so one fibre carries terabits per second. That is how one fibre between two Indian cities serves lakhs of calls and video streams.

blocks.text: FDM and WDM divide the spectrum, so nobody waits; TDM divides time, so everybody waits a little. Statistical TDM divides time on demand, so a slot's position no longer tells the receiver whose data it carries; every slot must carry an address.

examples.question: A T-1 style multiplexer combines 24 voice channels. Each is sampled 8000 times a second and encoded in 8 bits, and one framing bit is added per frame. Find (a) bits per frame, (b) frame rate and duration, (c) line bit rate, (d) bit rate per voice channel.
steps: (a) 24 × 8 = 192 payload bits; add the framing bit: 193 bits per frame.
(b) The frame rate equals the sampling rate: 8000 frames/s, so one frame lasts 1/8000 s = 125 µs.
examples.answer: 193 bits per frame at 8000 frames/s (125 µs), giving 1.544 Mbit/s; each voice channel gets 64 kbit/s.
examples.check:
channels = 24
bits = 8
rate = 8000
frame = channels * bits + 1
print(frame)
print(frame * rate)
print(rate, int(1e6/rate))
print(bits * rate)

examples.question: Four analog voice channels, each 4 kHz wide, are multiplexed by FDM with 1 kHz guard bands between adjacent channels. Find the total bandwidth. If the same channels use synchronous TDM with 8-bit samples at 8000 samples/s and one framing bit per frame, what line rate is needed?
steps: TDM per channel: 8 × 8000 = 64 kbit/s, so 4 channels give 256 kbit/s.
examples.answer: FDM needs 19 kHz; synchronous TDM needs 256 kbit/s of payload, or 264 kbit/s with framing.
examples.check:
channels = 4
bw = 4
guard = 1
print(channels * bw + (channels - 1) * guard)
bits = 8
rate = 8000
print(channels * bits * rate // 1000)
frame = channels * bits + 1
print(frame, frame * rate // 1000)

traps: Dropping the framing bit: 192 × 8000 = 1.536 Mbit/s instead of 193 × 8000 = 1.544 Mbit/s.
Multiplying frame size by bits per sample (193 × 8) instead of by the frame rate (193 × 8000). The multiplier is frames per second.
Writing n guard bands instead of n − 1; between n channels there are n − 1 gaps.
Mixing up frame and slot: a frame is one full round, a slot is one user's turn inside it.

Treating WDM as a new mechanism. It is FDM at optical frequencies, and wavelength and frequency are inversely related through f = c/λ, so a wavelength gap Δλ corresponds to a frequency gap Δf ≈ (c/λ²)·Δλ. Closer wavelengths (smaller Δλ) mean narrower bands in Hz, and the same Δλ gives a larger Δf at shorter wavelengths.

quiz.q: Define multiplexing and name the resource that FDM and TDM each divide.
quiz.a: Multiplexing combines several signals onto one link so its capacity is shared. FDM divides the frequency band; TDM divides time into slots.

quiz.q: How many bits are in a T-1 frame, and what is its line rate?
quiz.a: 24 × 8 + 1 = 193 bits. At 8000 frames/s the line rate is 193 × 8000 = 1.544 Mbit/s.

quiz.q: Why are guard bands needed in FDM, and why are they called wasteful?
quiz.a: Real filters cut off gradually, so a small unused gap stops one channel leaking into the next. The gap carries no data, so it is bandwidth paid for isolation: total = ΣB<sub>i</sub> + (n − 1)B<sub>guard</sub>.

quiz.q: Synchronous TDM sends no addresses, yet statistical TDM must. Why?
quiz.a: In synchronous TDM the slot position identifies the user every frame, so position is enough. In statistical TDM slots go to whoever has data, so position means nothing and each slot needs an address.

quiz.q: Eight voice channels of 4 kHz are multiplexed by FDM with 0.5 kHz guard bands between adjacent channels. Find the total bandwidth.
quiz.a: Channels: 8 × 4 kHz = 32 kHz. Guard bands: 7 × 0.5 kHz = 3.5 kHz. Total = 35.5 kHz.

quiz.q: An E-1 line sends 8000 frames per second with 32 slots of 8 bits each. Find the frame size, the line rate, and the number of voice channels carried.
quiz.a: Frame = 32 × 8 = 256 bits. Line rate = 256 × 8000 = 2.048 Mbit/s. Of the 32 slots, 30 carry voice at 64 kbit/s each and 2 carry framing and signalling.

quiz.q: A synchronous TDM link has 10 slots of 8 bits per frame at 8000 frames/s, but on average only 3 users have data. Compare it with statistical TDM for the same users.
quiz.a: Synchronous line rate = 10 × 8 × 8000 = 640 kbit/s, and 7 slots on average carry nothing, so only about 3/10 of the line is useful. Statistical TDM gives slots only to active users, so 640 kbit/s can serve many more users, while delay stays small as long as bursts stay below the slot count. The price is an address in every slot, buffering, and growing delay when many users burst together.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real optical backbones run DWDM with dozens of wavelengths on one fibre, and reconfigurable optical add-drop multiplexers (ROADMs) drop or add a whole wavelength at an intermediate city without converting it to electrical signals. Flexi-grid networks vary the spacing between wavelengths, the guard-band idea applied to light. The Optical Transport Network (OTN) wraps DWDM payloads with forward error correction and management overhead.
